value.overview: The White-fronted Nunbird (Monasa morphoeus) is a medium-sized, dark forest bird in the puffbird family. It has a conspicuous pale forehead and throat contrasting with its mostly blackish plumage, along with a stout, slightly hooked bill. This quiet, perch-watching species often lives in small groups and captures insects from exposed branches. Its broad distribution extends from southern Central America through much of northern and central South America.
value.classification: The White-fronted Nunbird belongs to the family Bucconidae, which includes puffbirds, nunlets, and nunbirds. Its scientific name is Monasa morphoeus.
value.identification: This nunbird is about 25 to 28 centimeters long. Adults are mainly sooty black or dark brown, with a broad white forehead, pale throat, and whitish to buffy markings on the breast. The bill is broad, heavy, and dark, while the tail is fairly long and rounded. In Costa Rica, it can be distinguished from other puffbirds by its dark body combined with the sharply contrasting pale front of the head and throat.
value.rangeHabitat: The White-fronted Nunbird occurs from eastern Honduras through Nicaragua, Costa Rica, and Panama, then southward into Colombia, Venezuela, Ecuador, Peru, Bolivia, Brazil, and adjacent regions. In Costa Rica it is a resident species, especially associated with humid lowland and foothill forest on the Caribbean slope, although it may also occur locally on the Pacific side. It uses mature evergreen forest, forest edges, second growth, and other wooded habitats with sufficient cover and large trees.
value.migrationStatus: Resident in Costa Rica and elsewhere across its range; it is not considered a long-distance migrant. Individuals may make local movements in response to food availability or habitat conditions.
value.breeding: In Costa Rica, breeding has been reported mainly from December through May. The species nests in cavities, usually in trees or other suitable woody structures, where the female lays a small clutch of eggs. As in other nunbirds, both members of a pair may participate in territory defense, incubation, and care of the young. Detailed information on nest-site selection and parental roles is limited in some parts of its range.
value.dietFeeding: The diet consists chiefly of insects and other arthropods, including beetles, grasshoppers, cicadas, and similar prey. Small fruits and other food items may also be taken. A bird commonly sits motionless on an exposed branch, watches the surrounding vegetation, and makes short, direct flights to seize prey from leaves, branches, or the air before returning to a perch.
value.behavior: White-fronted Nunbirds are often encountered in pairs or small, active groups. They spend much of the day moving through the middle and upper levels of wooded habitats, using repeated calls to maintain contact. Their flight is usually short and direct between perches. They can be inconspicuous despite their contrasting plumage, especially when quietly watching from shaded branches, but groups may become noticeable when calling or chasing insects together.

conservation.populationTrend: The global population size is not well quantified, but the species has a broad range and is not currently considered globally threatened. No reliable evidence indicates a significant global population decline.
